<description>
This improves our `Sock` test coverage following CVE-2026-117350.

This leaves out the test for the specific case that led to the OOM until we [fix `select()` reporting](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36688#issue-6085527087) for urgent data, but i'm also trying not to fight the last battle too much. Instead i focused on trying to pin down all invariants Claude and I could come up with that could be reasonably tested. This will help us understand our code better, and get more assurance we do not break some assumption a (security critical) caller may be relying on further down the road.

Another goal is to tie the events our fuzzing mock can report to the events each OS actually reports, and when. A follow-up will extend the mock to match what these tests pin down. This wouldn’t have caught the CVE-2026-117350 bug: it was in the very logic the mock replaces, so a fuzz target could only have found it if the mock had been written with that bug in mind. But the next bug may well be somewhere else, and a mock that can report everything the real socket APIs can, lets the fuzzer reach corner cases which may lack a proper unit test.

A lot more coverage could be added. I chose not to add tests specific to the logic used for trusted interfaces (Tor control, the SOCKS5 proxy, I2P SAM) or to a single platform. I also left out the test which led me to find https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36688#issuecomment-6509375262, as this needs to be fixed first.
</description>

<commits>
ad0802789b qa: pin down the socket readiness that callers of Sock::Wait() rely on

Test what Sock::Wait() and Sock::WaitMany() report, under a matrix of
different conditions about the state of the socket and the requested
events.

A few notable invariants exercised here:
- Only what's requested is reported (in particular, no unrequested
  RecvEvent when we took care not to ask for it, see CVE-2026-117350).
- Nothing readable means no RecvEvent (an idle connection never wakes a
  wait for receiving).
- A reset wakes a wait for SendEvent, and the send() fails for good.
- A reported event always means we can make progress (avoid spins).
- Wait() and WaitMany() are equivalent.

Readiness is level-triggered, so the tests first make sure that what the
peer did has arrived and then check what a wait reports. They do not
rely on anything not happening within some time, which would be brittle.

Where the select() and poll() backends differ, the difference is spelled
out in one place ahead of the tests, so that a change of backend has to
update it. Callers cope with these differences, except with known
quirks. For instance, Windows' select() fails when no socket requests
anything.

511352ebf5 qa: check that WaitMany() reports each socket's own events

With many connections in random states, each waiting for random events,
check that a single WaitMany() reports for each socket the events of
that socket.

eb1844e333 qa: check the timeouts of Sock::Wait() and Sock::WaitMany()

Without events, a wait returns true once its timeout expires and reports
nothing, also when a socket on which nothing is requested is readable.
Callers rely on it to pace their loops (net.cpp, httpserver.cpp) and to
detect a timeout (ConnectToSocket() in netbase.cpp, i2p.cpp, pcp.cpp).

A negative timeout is not tested: poll() would wait forever and select()
fails. No caller passes one.

Remove the wait test: it exercises strictly less than the long_timeout
test introduced in this commit.

bc94b13a1e qa: check what a listening socket reports

A listening socket reports RecvEvent when, and only when, accept() will
succeed. net.cpp accepts one connection per wake-up and httpserver.cpp
accepts until accept() fails.

931ed60d4a qa: check what a non-blocking connect() reports

A non-blocking connect() that succeeds, or that is refused, wakes up a
wait for RecvEvent | SendEvent and SO_ERROR then tells the outcome, as
ConnectToSocket() expects.

f62b338c9e qa: check that socket readiness is level-triggered

What is left after a partial read, and then the end of the stream, are
reported again. net.cpp reads at most 64 KiB per wake-up and relies on
this.

cbfd01494d qa: pin down the options of CreateSockOS() and accepted sockets

Check that CreateSockOS() sockets are non-blocking and have TCP_NODELAY
and, where it exists, SO_NOSIGPIPE, and which of these a socket accepted
from one inherits.

net.cpp and httpserver.cpp do not make accepted sockets non-blocking.
On Linux they are not, as accept() does not pass O_NONBLOCK on, and the
callers rely on MSG_DONTWAIT instead. Check that Recv() and Send() with
MSG_DONTWAIT return would-block rather than wait on a socket as accept()
returns it. Where MSG_DONTWAIT does not exist (Windows), check at compile
time that accepted sockets inherit non-blocking mode, and at run time
that they do.
</commits>
